turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. ____. Nice to meet you. Well... honestly, I'm just at my wit's end, which is why I finally made this appointment. I've been a carpenter for years, mostly custom cabinetry and some framing, and you really need to be sharp for that, you know? Measure twice, cut once, all that. But what brings me in is I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. It's like... it's like my brain just won't stay put. 

I'll be right in the middle of routing an edge or reading a blueprint, and just one saw starting up across the shop—or even just somebody walking past the office window with a cup of coffee—and that's it. My focus is entirely broken. It pulls me right off what I'm doing. And sometimes it's not even something happening around me, it's just my own head. A thought about another job we're supposed to start next week will pop up, and suddenly I'm completely derailed. I'll put down my tools to go check the lumber order for that other job, and then on the way I'll see a sander that needs a new pad, and I'll start fixing that... and then, well, the whole day just gets away from me. I look at the clock and it's 4 PM and I haven't finished the one simple task I started at 8 AM. It's so incredibly frustrating, and I just can't seem to stop it from happening, no matter how hard I try to just buckle down and do my work.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports an inability to keep their mind on one thing and difficulty sustaining focus on their work tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish workplace duties, noting they often haven't finished a simple task started at 8 AM by the end of the day.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (a saw starting, someone walking by) and unrelated thoughts (thinking about another job).

turns.doctor_question: Did these concentration and distractibility problems start when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes. I mean, it's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about my mother the other day and how frustrated she used to get with me about this exact kind of thing. Even way back in grade school—definitely way before I was, I don't know, 11 or 12 years old—it was always the exact same story at every single parent-teacher conference. 

I can still picture my fourth-grade classroom, you know, with those old heavy wooden desks? Anyway, my teachers were always, *always* pulling my mother aside or writing these long notes sent home in my folder, telling her that I was a bright girl, that I had a lot of potential, but that I was just so incredibly careless. That was the word they loved to use. Careless. I'd sit and do my homework at the kitchen table while my mom cooked dinner, I know I did it, but then by the time I actually got to school the next morning, it was just... gone. Lost somewhere in the bottom of my backpack, or I left it on the kitchen counter, or it fell out on the bus. 

And forgetting instructions? Forget about it. The teacher would stand at the chalkboard and give us three simple things to do, and I'd maybe hear the first half of the first thing before my brain just went somewhere else entirely. I'd spend half the afternoon just staring out the window, watching the cars go by or looking at the trees blowing in the wind, instead of finishing the seatwork right in front of me. My mom used to sit me down at the kitchen table and say, "Why can't you just finish your math worksheet like the other kids?" and I never had a good answer for her. I really didn't. It's just like my brain was on a completely different channel, and it's been exactly like that for as long as I can remember, really. It just feels so much worse now because, well, the stakes are a lot higher when you're building a custom staircase compared to filling out a spelling workbook, you know? But yes, it's been happening since I was a little girl.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that her teachers frequently described her as being 'incredibly careless' with her work.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks, spending half the afternoon staring out the window instead of doing seatwork.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly mentions forgetting instructions and failing to finish schoolwork, such as math worksheets.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient frequently lost her completed homework, leaving it on the counter or losing it in her backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as watching cars go by or trees blowing in the wind.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also feel unusually restless or fidgety, as if you have to be moving or can’t sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s more of an internal thing for me, if that makes sense? People always think of someone literally bouncing off the walls, and since I'm on my feet all day in the shop anyway, I'm already moving a lot. But when I actually *have* to sit down... oh boy. 

Like, if I have to sit at the desk in the back office doing estimates—which I have to do a lot of, pricing out materials and trying to get all the numbers straight for the clients—or if I have to sit through one of those long, drawn-out meetings with the general contractors... I just get this awful feeling. I get completely wound up inside. It’s like this tight, buzzing feeling in my chest and my legs, like I absolutely *need* to get up and move around right that very second. 

And the silly thing is, I actually hurt my wrist a while back, so I had to take it easy on the heavy lifting and do more of the office work for a bit. But even now, my wrist is completely healed, perfectly fine, and I know I’m supposed to just stay put at that desk and finish the paperwork. I tell myself, "Just sit here and finish this one bid," but the longer I sit there, the more that wound-up feeling builds and builds. I just feel so incredibly restless, like my skin is crawling, and I almost always end up getting up and pacing around the office or going out to the shop floor just to walk it off, even though I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish what's in front of me. It's exhausting, honestly.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they almost always end up getting up and pacing around the office when they are supposed to stay put at their desk and finish paperwork.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense internal feeling of being 'wound up' and 'incredibly restless' with a strong need to get up and move around when forced to sit.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often act impulsively, like blurting things out or making decisions without thinking them through?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I know some people are like that, just jumping into things without looking, but that's never really been my problem. If anything, I probably think about things too much, you know? Like, when I'm looking at a set of plans, I'll stare at them for hours trying to figure out the absolute best way to cut the sheet goods so I don't waste any material. Plywood is so expensive right now—I mean, you wouldn't believe what a single sheet of cabinet-grade birch costs these days, it's highway robbery. So I'll sit there and draw out all these different cutting diagrams, and I'll get so lost in trying to make it perfect that I end up burning half the day just planning and not actually making any sawdust. 

And as for blurting things out... no, I don't think I do that. In fact, when I'm in those meetings with the contractors I mentioned earlier, I usually have the opposite problem. I'll have a thought about how we really need to change the framing around a bay window because the specs they gave us just aren't going to hold the weight right, and I'll sit there trying to figure out the exact right way to say it so I don't sound like I'm stepping on anyone's toes. By the time I actually get my thoughts organized enough to speak up, they've already moved on to talking about the plumbing rough-in or the electrical schedule, and I've completely missed my chance. So no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. It's really just the focus... just keeping my brain on the track it's supposed to be on, instead of letting it wander off into the weeds.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient admits to struggling with focus and keeping their brain on the track it is supposed to be on.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes their mind wandering off 'into the weeds', indicating distractibility by unrelated thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies blurting things out or acting impulsively.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also often fidget, squirm, or feel unable to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean, like I was just saying about the restless feeling... I don't know if I'd call it fidgeting, exactly. I mean, when I think of fidgeting, I think of my nephew, little Tommy, who's always tapping his pencil or bouncing his knee under the dinner table so hard the whole table shakes and my sister has to yell at him to stop. I don't really do that kind of thing. 

I mean, sure, if I'm stuck at that desk doing the estimates like I mentioned, I might chew on the end of my pen, or I might sort of shift my weight from side to side in the chair because the lumbar support on that thing is completely shot. I've been meaning to buy a new office chair for three years now, but every time I go to the office supply store, I get distracted by the power tools next door at the hardware store and completely forget why I went out in the first place. But anyway, I don't think I'm visibly squirming or anything like that. It's really just that internal buzzing feeling I was talking about. 

I guess maybe I do get up and walk around more than I should when I'm supposed to be sitting. Like, I'll tell myself I just need to go check the mail, or I need to go see if the glue on those cabinet joints is dry yet, even though I know perfectly well it needs another four hours. I just find any excuse to get out of that chair. So I don't know if that counts as not being able to sit still, or if it's just me finding ways to avoid the paperwork because my brain just absolutely refuses to focus on the numbers. But as far as actually sitting there and squirming like a little kid? No, I don't think I really do that.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient states their brain 'absolutely refuses to focus on the numbers', indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient admits to 'finding ways to avoid the paperwork', showing reluctance to engage in tasks requiring sustained mental effort.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions getting 'distracted by the power tools next door' when trying to run an errand.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient notes they 'completely forget why I went out in the first place' when running errands.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits they 'get up and walk around more than I should when I'm supposed to be sitting' and find 'any excuse to get out of that chair'.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes experiencing an 'internal buzzing feeling' and a 'restless feeling'.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies fidgeting or squirming, stating 'I don't really do that kind of thing' and 'squirming like a little kid? No, I don't think I really do that.'

turns.doctor_question: Do you often lose things you need for tasks, like tools, paperwork, or keys?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, all the time. It’s actually becoming a real problem at the shop. I mean, it sounds like such a small thing, right? Misplacing a pencil or whatever. But it’s not just a pencil. I am constantly—and I mean constantly—hunting for things I *just* had in my hand. 

Like my tape measure. You’d think a carpenter would keep her tape measure clipped to her belt, right? And I do! Or, well, I try to. But I’ll pull it off to measure a piece of trim, and then someone will ask me a question about the delivery schedule, and I’ll set the tape down on a stack of drywall. Then I go back to the trim, and the tape is gone. I’ll spend twenty minutes walking around the shop, looking on every workbench, inside the toolboxes, even checking the break room just in case I took it in there when I went to get coffee. And it’s not just the tape measure. It’s my keys, my phone, the order sheets... 

Oh Lord, the order sheets. Just last Tuesday, we had this massive delivery of custom millwork coming in for that big Victorian renovation downtown. I had the packing slip right in my hand, I swear I did. I was checking off the boxes as the guys unloaded them. Then the phone rang—it was the client, wanting to change the stain color on the stair treads at the absolute last minute, which is a whole other headache because once you apply that dark walnut, there’s no going back—and when I hung up, the packing slip was just... gone. Poof. I tore the office apart. I was looking under the desk, digging through the trash can, checking the clipboard where it’s *supposed* to be. 

It eats up so much of the day. Honestly, I probably lose an hour or two every single shift just walking in circles looking for things. It’s gotten so bad that the guys on the crew have started checking behind me. Like, if I walk away from a saw, Dave—he's my shop foreman, great guy, been with me for fifteen years—Dave will actually walk over and pick up my safety glasses or my notes before I can lose them. He jokes about it, says he’s my personal retriever, but I know it frustrates him. And it frustrates me! I’m 57 years old, I run a whole business, I should be able to keep track of a piece of paper or my own car keys. But I just set things down without even registering that I’m doing it, and then my brain just completely wipes the memory of where they went.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly confirms constantly losing necessary items for her work, such as her tape measure, keys, phone, and order sheets.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a coworker asking a question or the phone ringing, which causes her to lose track of what she was doing and misplace items.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did you already have these attention or restlessness problems in more than one setting, like both at school and at home?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely. It’s funny you ask about being a kid, because I was actually just talking to my older sister about this the other day. Even way back in grade school, I mean, well before I was twelve... probably starting in second or third grade, it was always the exact same story. 

My mother—God rest her soul, she was an absolute saint for putting up with me—she used to just dread those parent-teacher conferences. Every single year, she’d go in and sit in those tiny little chairs, and the teachers would tell her the exact same thing. They'd say, "She’s a bright girl, she really is, but she's just so careless." That was always the word they used. Careless. Because I was always losing my homework. I’d sit at the kitchen table, I’d actually do the math worksheet, and then... I don't know, it would just vanish between the kitchen and my desk at school. Just like those packing slips at the shop now! 

And when I was actually in the classroom, sitting there during seatwork time when we were supposed to be practicing our multiplication tables or cursive or whatever? I wouldn't be doing it. I’d be staring straight out the window. Our school had these big old oak trees right outside the classroom—beautiful trees, really old, you could just tell they had gorgeous tight grain under the bark—and I would just watch the branches moving in the wind for what felt like hours. The teacher would have to snap her fingers to get me to look back at my paper, and by then, the period was over and my seatwork was completely blank. 

And it wasn’t just at school, either, which is why my mom was always so frustrated. It was at home, too. She would give me a few simple instructions, like... take out the trash, feed the dog, and put my shoes in the closet. Basic stuff, right? And I’d go to do them, and I’d get the trash bag out, but then I’d see a loose board on the back porch and start messing with it, and next thing you know, the dog isn't fed, my shoes are still right in the middle of the hallway where people can trip over them, and the trash is just sitting on the kitchen floor. I just forgot the instructions the absolute second they left her mouth. So, yeah, it’s been exactly like this my entire life. It’s exhausting, really, thinking about how long I've been fighting my own brain. You'd think by 57 I'd have figured out a system, but... well, I guess that's why I'm sitting here talking to you.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that her teachers described her as 'careless' during her childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes being unable to focus on seatwork, instead staring out the window for long periods.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states she failed to finish schoolwork (blank seatwork) and did not follow through on chores like taking out the trash or feeding the dog.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient notes she was 'always losing my homework' before she could turn it in.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as trees outside the window or a loose board on the porch.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions forgetting simple instructions for daily chores the moment they were given.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever done things impulsively without thinking first, like interrupting people, blurting out answers, or making snap decisions you later regretted?
turns.patient_response:
Impulsive? No, I don't think so. I mean, when I think of impulsive, I think of people who just jump right into things without looking, right? Like, you get these young guys on the job site who just start cutting into a beautiful piece of mahogany without measuring twice or checking the grain direction. That is a real quick way to ruin a thousand dollars of wood, let me tell you, and I would never do that. 

If anything, I'm the exact opposite of impulsive. I'll stand there staring at the wood, trying to plan the cut, and then I'll start thinking about whether the table saw blade needs sharpening, and then I'm walking away to look for the sharpening tools, and... well, you know how that goes, I just told you about my tape measure. So I'm definitely not making snap decisions. I take forever to make a decision because I just get completely derailed before I can even make one. 

And as for interrupting people or blurting things out? Not really. I'm usually so lost in my own head during a conversation that I don't even have a chance to interrupt. If someone is talking to me, especially if it's a long story or a complicated client request, I'm usually just trying so hard to force my brain to follow along. Or, honestly, my mind has already drifted off and I'm thinking about whether I remembered to lock the loading dock doors at the shop. 

People actually get mad at me for *not* responding fast enough, rather than me talking over them. They'll ask me a question and I just kind of stare blankly for a second while my brain tries to rewind and figure out what they just said. My ex-husband used to absolutely hate that. He'd say, "Are you even in there? Are you listening to me?" And I was! I really was trying to, but I just couldn't process it fast enough to blurt anything out, let alone interrupt him. So no, I wouldn't say I have that problem of speaking out of turn or doing things on a whim. I'm too busy just trying to keep my head above water to be spontaneous like that.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes struggling to follow along when spoken to, drifting off during conversations, and being accused of not listening.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes getting easily derailed by unrelated thoughts (e.g., thinking about sharpening tools or locking doors) while trying to focus on a task or conversation.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies blurting things out, stating they process information too slowly to speak out of turn.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting people, noting they are usually too lost in their own head to do so.
